StringWithMarkup.String: The major hazards encountered in the use and handling of bischloromethyl ketone stem from its toxicologic properties. Toxic by all routes (ie, inhalation, ingestion, and dermal absorption), exposure to this crystalline substance may occur from its use as vesicant or in the synthesis of citric acid. Effects from exposure may include contact burns to the skin and eyes, and even death with sufficiently high concentrations. In activities or situations where over exposure may occur, wear a self-contained breathing apparatus and chemical protective clothing which is specifically recommended by the shipper or producer. If contact should occur. immediately flush affected skin or eyes with running water for at least 15 minutes, and remove contaminated clothing and shoes at the site. While bischloromethyl ketone does not ignite easily, it may burn with the production of irritating and poisonous gases. Also, containers may explode violently in the heat of a fire. Fires involving bischloromethyl ketone may be extinguished with dry chemical, CO2, Halon, water spray, fog, or standard foam. Fight the fire from as far a distance as possible, and dike runoff from fire control water. Containers for international shipment by air and water must bear the labels, "Corrosive" and "Poison", respectively. Small spills of bischloromethyl ketone may be taken up and placed into containers for later disposal (liquid solutions are first absorbed by sand or other noncombustible material). Large liquid spills should be diked far ahead of the spill area for later disposal. Prior to implementing land disposal of bischloromethyl ketone, consult with environmental regulatory agencies for guidance.

Signs and Symptoms of Bis(chloromethyl) Ketone Exposure: Signs and symptoms of acute exposure to bis(chloromethyl) ketone include burning of the skin and mucous membrane surfaces. Eye exposure may result in pain, lacrimation (tearing), and corneal damage. Tachycardia (rapid heart beat), hypothermia (low body temperature), nausea and vomiting may also be noted. Skin exposure to the liquid or vapor may result in dermatitis and paresthesia (burning or prickling sensation) of affected areas. CNS depression may be noted following inhalation. Headache, dizziness, fainting, tremor, and coma are also potential symptoms.

Reference.Description: An organic chemistry ontology developed by MolGenie and OntoChem to assign chemical entities to structural classes, split into three main subsections: calculated properties, compounds and substructural concepts. The ontology contains chemistry structural classes with a focus on elements and small organic compounds, but not inorganic, polymer, biopolymer, metal complexes, metal organic frameworks (MOFs) and other chemistry entities. The ontology has been mapped to several collections of chemicals, including (a) Chemicals of Biological Interest (ChEBI), (b) the ChEMBL database of bioactive molecules, (c) the LOTUS natural product collection, (d) per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) extracted from Barnabas et al (2022) DOI: 10.1039/D2DD00019A (e) PubChemLite and (f) the ZeroPM Global Chemical Inventory.
